questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with a painless genital ulcer with indurated edges and a clean base. Inguinal lymphadenopathy is firm and non-tender. Dark-field microscopy reveals motile spirochetes. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (Treponema pallidum) is treated with Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM as a single dose — the CDC and WHO first-line recommendation. Doxycycline is for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman develops painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the labia majora, 5 days after a new sexual partner. She had a similar episode 6 months ago. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. What is the treatment for recurrent episodes?
questions.exp: Recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2) episodic therapy: Valacyclovir 500 mg BD for 3 days (or 1g OD for 5 days) is the preferred short-course option. Famciclovir 1500 mg single dose is also effective but less commonly used.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child presents with multiple circular scaly patches on the scalp with broken-off hair stubs (black dots). KOH mount shows endothrix spores. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Endothrix invasion (spores within the hair shaft) with black-dot pattern is caused by Trichophyton tonsurans and T. violaceum. T. tonsurans is the most common cause of black-dot tinea capitis, especially in urban settings. M. canis causes ectothrix infection.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer presents with a painless nodule on the dorsum of the hand that ulcerated and discharged granules. Histopathology shows a grain with a Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon (eosinophilic material surrounding organisms) is seen in actinomycetoma (caused by filamentous bacteria like Nocardia and Actinomadura). Eumycetoma is caused by true fungi. The farmer exposure supports actinomycetoma.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man with type 1 lepra reaction presents with fever, tender erythematous nodules on the limbs, and painful eyes. His leprosy was diagnosed 1 year ago and he is on MDT. What is the best treatment for the acute reaction?
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction is treated with systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 40-60 mg/day). Thalidomide is used for ENL (Type 2 reaction, erythema nodosum leprosum) but is contraindicated in women of childbearing age. Clofazimine is used adjunctively for ENL.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with hypopigmented anaesthetic patches on the back. Slit-skin smear is negative. Nerve thickening is present unilaterally. According to WHO classification, which regimen should be used?
questions.exp: Patients with 1-5 skin lesions and negative smears are classified as paucibacillary (PB) leprosy by WHO. PB-MDT consists of rifampicin 600 mg monthly + dapsone 100 mg daily for 6 months.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with a butterfly-shaped erythematous rash on the face, joint pain, and oral ulcers. ANA is positive (1:320), anti-dsDNA is elevated, and complement C3/C4 are low. Which skin finding is MOST specific for her diagnosis?
questions.exp: Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) lesions with follicular plugging, atrophic scarring, and hypopigmentation are specific to lupus erythematosus. Gottron's papules are pathognomonic for dermatomyositis. Periungual telangiectasia is seen in connective tissue disorders generally.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with progressive skin tightening, Raynaud's phenomenon, and dysphagia. Calcinosis cutis is present on the fingertips. Anti-Scl-70 antibody is positive. Which is the most likely complication causing mortality?
questions.exp: Diffuse systemic sclerosis with anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension, which is the leading cause of mortality. Anti-centromere antibody is associated with limited SSc (CREST syndrome) and PAH.

questions.q: A neonate develops flaccid blisters at sites of minor trauma. Nikolsky's sign is positive. Skin biopsy shows sub-epidermal blister with cleavage at the lamina lucida. Electron microscopy reveals reduced hemidesmosomes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Junctional EB (Herlitz type) shows cleavage within the lamina lucida on EM with reduced/absent hemidesmosomes. Mutations are in LAMA3, LAMB3, LAMC2 (laminin-332) genes. Dystrophic EB shows cleavage below the lamina densa due to collagen VII mutations.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman presents with tense blisters on normal skin and urticated plaques. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. ELISA is positive for BP180. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (anti-BP180 IgG) is treated with systemic corticosteroids as first-line therapy. Doxycycline + nicotinamide is an alternative for mild disease. Rituximab is reserved for refractory cases.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with flaccid blisters on the oral mucosa and skin. Blisters rupture easily leaving raw erosions. DIF shows intercellular IgG deposits (chicken-wire pattern). ELISA confirms anti-desmoglein 3 antibodies. Which drug is the anchor therapy?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris is treated with systemic corticosteroids as the mainstay (anchor) therapy, usually combined with a steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine or MMF). Rituximab is increasingly used as first-line for severe disease, but prednisolone remains the anchor.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with a pearly translucent papule with rolled edges and telangiectasia on the nose. It has been slowly enlarging for 2 years. Which histopathological feature is characteristic?
opts: Palisading of nuclei at the periphery of tumour islands
Asymmetric nests of melanocytes at the DEJ
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading of nuclei and retraction artefact. Horn pearls are seen in squamous cell carcinoma. Pagetoid spread is seen in Paget's disease and MIS.

questions.q: A 65-year-old immunosuppressed renal transplant patient develops a rapidly growing keratotic nodule on the dorsum of the hand. Biopsy shows atypical squamous cells invading the dermis with individual cell keratinisation. What is the most common risk factor in this population?
questions.exp: In organ transplant recipients, HPV (especially oncogenic types 5 and 8 of beta-HPV genus) plays a major role in SCC development alongside UV radiation and immunosuppression. The cumulative incidence of SCC is dramatically elevated post-transplant.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with a dark-brown pigmented lesion on the sole (1.5 cm) with irregular borders. Dermoscopy shows a parallel ridge pattern. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM) on acral sites (palm/sole/subungual) shows a parallel ridge pattern on dermoscopy (pigmentation in the ridges, not the furrows). This contrasts with benign melanocytic nevi which show parallel furrow pattern.

questions.q: During Mohs micrographic surgery, after excision of a skin cancer, horizontal frozen sections reveal tumour at one margin. What is the next step?
opts: Re-excise only the positive margin with another Mohs stage
Convert to wide local excision with 1 cm margin
Send the specimen for permanent paraffin sections
Apply curettage and electrodesiccation to the area
questions.exp: The defining feature of Mohs surgery is tissue-sparing: only the margin that is positive for tumour is re-excised in the next stage. This maximises normal tissue preservation while achieving complete margin control with 100% sectioning.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman undergoes patch testing. At 48 hours, she shows a +2 reaction to nickel sulfate. At 96-hour reading, the reaction has increased in size and intensity. What does this suggest?
opts: False positive due to patch pressure
questions.exp: In allergic contact dermatitis (Type IV hypersensitivity), the patch test reaction typically increases from 48h to 96h (crescendo pattern). Irritant reactions tend to peak at 48h and then fade (decrescendo pattern). Increasing reaction is a hallmark of true allergy.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman is prescribed dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis. Two weeks later she develops haemolytic anaemia. Which enzyme deficiency predisposes to this complication?
questions.exp: Dapsone causes oxidative haemolysis, which is markedly worsened in G6PD-deficient individuals. G6PD screening is recommended before starting dapsone. TPMT deficiency predisposes to azathioprine toxicity (myelosuppression).

questions.q: A patient on methotrexate for psoriasis requires monitoring for hepatotoxicity. Which investigation provides the most reliable assessment of cumulative hepatic damage?
opts: Liver biopsy after every 1.5 g cumulative dose
questions.exp: PIIINP (procollagen III aminoterminal peptide) is a serum marker of hepatic fibrosis and is the preferred non-invasive monitoring method for MTX-induced liver disease in dermatology, replacing routine liver biopsies. Persistently elevated levels indicate biopsy is needed.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis fails two biologics. She is started on secukinumab. What is the mechanism of action?
questions.exp: Secukinumab is a fully human anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody. Ustekinumab targets the p40 subunit shared by IL-12 and IL-23. Guselkumab/risankizumab target the p19 subunit of IL-23 specifically. Adalimumab and infliximab are anti-TNF agents.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with itchy papules over the flexures and a personal history of asthma and hay fever. Her mother has eczema. On exam, there is lichenification with excoriation in the antecubital fossae. Which immunological profile is most characteristic?
questions.exp: Atopic dermatitis is characterised by Th2 immune deviation (IL-4, IL-13, IL-31) leading to elevated total IgE and allergen-specific IgE. This drives IgE-mediated sensitisation and mast cell activation. Dupilumab targets the shared IL-4Rα receptor blocking both IL-4 and IL-13.

questions.q: A 14-year-old girl develops a widespread vesicular eruption 2 days after contact with poison ivy during a school trip. The rash is linear and vesicular on exposed parts. What type of hypersensitivity reaction is this?
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis from urushiol (poison ivy antigen) is a classic Type IV (T-cell mediated, delayed) hypersensitivity reaction, occurring 24-96 hours after exposure. T-cells sensitised during prior exposure release cytokines on re-exposure causing the vesicular eruption.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man with chronic alcohol use develops porphyria cutanea tarda. He presents with skin fragility, blistering on sun-exposed areas, and hypertrichosis on the temples. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.exp: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) results from deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD), leading to accumulation of uroporphyrin I in skin. This causes photosensitivity, skin fragility, and hypertrichosis. Ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria.

questions.q: A 30-year-old pregnant woman at 32 weeks presents with intensely pruritic urticarial papules and plaques around the umbilicus that spare the umbilicus itself. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: PEP (Polymorphic Eruption of Pregnancy, formerly PUPPP) starts in abdominal striae and classically spares the umbilicus. Pemphigoid gestationis typically starts periumbilically and is associated with anti-BP180 IgG. PEP carries no fetal risk unlike pemphigoid gestationis.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with diffuse hyperpigmentation in sun-exposed and unexposed areas, hypotension, and fatigue. She was on long-term prednisolone for asthma that was recently stopped abruptly. Which skin finding is expected?
questions.exp: Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) from abrupt steroid withdrawal causes elevated ACTH/MSH, leading to generalised hyperpigmentation including mucous membranes (buccal, gingival), palmar creases, and pressure areas. This distinguishes it from secondary causes.

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman presents with depigmented macules on the dorsum of both hands with leukotrichia. Wood's lamp shows bright-white fluorescence. Which cells are destroyed in this condition?
questions.exp: Vitiligo results from selective destruction of melanocytes by autoimmune T-cell-mediated mechanisms. Wood's lamp accentuates the depigmentation (bright white fluorescence). Leukotrichia indicates destruction of follicular melanocytes and implies poor repigmentation potential.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis presents with palpable purpura on the lower limbs. Skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits in vessel walls. Which diagnosis does this suggest?
questions.exp: IgA vasculitis (HSP) is defined by IgA-dominant immune deposits in vessel walls affecting small vessels. It presents with palpable purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain, and renal involvement. Although more common in children, it can occur in adults with RA as a trigger.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with recurrent crops of erythematous papules and vesicles with excoriations on the elbows, knees, and buttocks. Immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits at the dermoepidermal junction. What is the associated systemic disease?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is pathognomonic of gluten-sensitive enteropathy (coeliac disease). Granular IgA deposits in dermal papillae are diagnostic. Gluten-free diet improves both the skin and gut disease. Dapsone controls the skin manifestation.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with multiple coffee-au-lait macules (>6, each >1.5 cm), axillary freckling, and multiple soft skin-coloured pedunculated tumours on the trunk. His child has similar lesions. Which gene is mutated?
questions.exp: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is caused by mutations in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17q11.2, encoding neurofibromin (a GTPase-activating protein). It is autosomal dominant. NF2 mutations on chromosome 22 cause bilateral acoustic neuromas without CALMs.

questions.q: A 34-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 count 80 cells/μL) presents with red-purple papules and nodules on the lower limbs, oral cavity, and palate. Biopsy shows proliferating spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces and HHV-8 antigens. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: AIDS-associated Kaposi's sarcoma (epidemic KS) — the first-line treatment is HAART, which restores immune function and leads to regression in many patients. Liposomal doxorubicin is first-line for advanced or rapidly progressive disease requiring systemic chemotherapy.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with a 3-year history of non-scarring hair loss in a band-like pattern at the frontotemporal margin. He denies systemic symptoms. Dermoscopy shows peripilar casts and brown halos around follicular openings at the hairline. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Frontal fibrosing alopecia (FFA) is a form of lichen planopilaris presenting as slowly progressive band-like frontal hairline recession with peripilar casts and perifollicular erythema. Though classically in postmenopausal women, it increasingly affects younger men. Dermoscopy shows follicular dropout.
